entry: Private research university in [[New York City]], chartered in 1831 as the University of the City of New York, with Albert Gallatin as its first president. The main campus is in Greenwich Village around Washington Square Park, with an engineering school in [[Brooklyn]] and graduate schools throughout [[Manhattan]]. NYU enrolled 61,890 students in 2023. Its global system includes degree-granting portal campuses in [[Abu Dhabi]] and [[Shanghai]]. Past and present faculty and alumni include 39 Nobel laureates and 26 [[Pulitzer Prize]] winners.

[[Major League Baseball]] franchise based in the Bronx, [[New York City]]. Founded in 1903 as the New York Highlanders, the team was renamed the Yankees in 1913. The Yankees have won 27 [[World Series]] championships, a Major League Baseball record, and 52 players and 11 managers have been inducted into the National Baseball Hall of Fame, including [[Babe Ruth]] and [[Lou Gehrig]]. According to [[Forbes]], the Yankees are the most valuable Major League Baseball franchise. Their rivalry with the [[Boston Red Sox]] is one of the best known in North American sports.

U.S. state in the Northeastern United States and one of the original [[Thirteen Colonies]]. It has over 20 million residents and a total area of 141,300 sq km (54,556 sq mi). New York borders [[New England]], Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Canada, and extends into the Atlantic Ocean and the Great Lakes. Downstate, including [[New York City]] and Long Island, holds about two-thirds of the population. The Dutch established the colony of New Netherland in 1621, and England seized it in 1664. The state ratified the U.S. Constitution in 1788. Development of its interior, beginning with the [[Erie Canal]] in the early 19th century, earned it the nickname "Empire State". About 200 colleges and universities include [[Columbia University]] and [[Cornell University]], both Ivy League members.

Island country in the southwestern [[Pacific Ocean]], east of [[Australia]] across the Tasman Sea. It consists of the [[North Island]], the [[South Island]] and many smaller islands. The capital is [[Wellington]], and the largest city is Auckland. Polynesians settled the islands between about 1280 and 1350 and developed a distinctive Māori culture. The Dutch explorer [[Abel Tasman]] was the first European to record the islands, in 1642, and [[James Cook]] was the first to map them, in 1769. After the Treaty of Waitangi was signed with Māori chiefs in 1840, Britain declared sovereignty and the Colony of New Zealand was established in 1841. New Zealand became a dominion in 1907 and gained full statutory independence in 1947. It was the first country to introduce a minimum wage and to give women the right to vote. Its population is around 5.3 million.

entry: Men's [[Rugby union]] team of [[New Zealand]], known as the All Blacks. The team won the [[Rugby World Cup]] in 1987, 2011 and 2015, and was the first country to retain the title. Its first international test was against Australia in [[Sydney]] in 1903. The name "All Blacks" dates from its 1905 tour, when the team wore all black. Traditionally, the All Blacks perform the haka Ka Mate before matches.

Religious or spiritual group of modern origin that is peripheral to its society's dominant religious culture. Such groups, also called new religions, number in the tens of thousands worldwide, and most have only a few members. Scholars differ on the starting point, from the 1950s or 1945 to 1830, when [[Joseph Smith]] founded the Latter Day Saint movement. The 1893 Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago included movements such as [[Christian Science]] and the [[Baháʼí Faith]]. Established religions and secular institutions have often opposed new religions, and Western anti-cult and Christian countercult movements emerged in the 1970s and 1980s. Scholars often explain their rise through secularization, globalization and individualization.

Most populous city in [[New Jersey]] and county seat of Essex County (pop., 2020: 311,549). Settled in 1666 by [[Puritans]] from New Haven Colony, it is one of the oldest cities in the United States and a principal city of the New York metropolitan area. Its port, Port Newark–Elizabeth, is the primary container terminal of the busiest seaport on the U.S. East Coast. Newark Liberty International Airport was the first municipal commercial airport in the United States. Companies headquartered in Newark include Prudential, PSEG and [[Panasonic|Panasonic Corporation of North America]].

City and metropolitan borough in Tyne and Wear, England's northernmost city (pop., 2025 est.: 320,838). It developed around the Roman fort and bridge of Pons Aelius, named for the family name of the Roman emperor [[Hadrian]], and fragments of [[Hadrian's Wall]] are visible in parts of the city. In 1080 Robert Curthose, son of [[William the Conqueror]], built a wooden castle there, and the town became known as New Castle. It was one of the world's largest [[Shipbuilding|shipbuilding]] and ship repair centers during the [[Industrial Revolution]].

Easternmost province of [[Canada]], in the Atlantic region (pop., 2026: 552,462). It comprises the island of [[Newfoundland (island)|Newfoundland]] and the mainland region of Labrador, which has a land border with [[Quebec]]. In 2021, 99.4% of residents reported English as their native language, making it Canada's most linguistically homogeneous province. Until 1949 it was the separate Dominion of Newfoundland within the [[British Empire]]. After the [[Great Depression]], the House of Assembly voted in 1933 to dissolve itself in favor of a British-appointed Commission of Government. The province joined Canada on March 31, 1949, as its tenth province.

Large island off the eastern coast of North America, part of the Canadian province of [[Newfoundland and Labrador]]. At 108,878.06 sq km, it is Canada's fourth-largest island and the world's fifteenth-largest. The island is separated from Labrador by the Strait of Belle Isle and from Cape Breton Island by the Cabot Strait, and it blocks the mouth of the [[St. Lawrence River]]. It had 510,550 residents in the 2021 census. Norse explorers built a temporary base at L'Anse aux Meadows, dated to about 1000 years ago. On August 5, 1583, Humphrey Gilbert claimed the island for England under a royal charter of [[Elizabeth I]], making it Britain's oldest colony, a forerunner of the [[British Empire]].

Information about current events, distributed through word of mouth, printing, broadcasting, electronic communication or witnesses. Subjects include war, government, politics, health, economy, business, sport and entertainment, as well as unusual events. Government proclamations about royal ceremonies, laws, taxes and public health have been called news since ancient times. Newspapers developed in China over centuries and became established in Europe during the early modern period. In the 20th century, [[Radio]] and [[Television]] became important means of transmitting news, and in the 21st century the [[Internet]] has begun to play a similar role. Most news organizations value impartiality, neutrality and objectivity, despite the difficulty of reporting without political bias. The phrase "current events" was coined by Jessica Garretson Finch while teaching at Barnard College in the 1890s.

Forms of [[Mass media]] that focus on delivering news to the general public, including news agencies, newspapers, news magazines and news channels. Some of the first news circulated in Renaissance Europe in handwritten newsletters among merchants. After the printing press was invented by [[Johannes Gutenberg]] in 1440, newspapers could be mass-produced cheaply. The first newspaper written in English, The Weekly News, was published in London in 1621. In 1729, [[Benjamin Franklin]] began writing a more satirical kind of newspaper in the [[United States]]. In the 1830s, newspapers turned toward commercial success and reportage, beginning with the New York Sun in 1833. In the early 1920s, radio allowed large audiences to hear breaking news simultaneously. The Communications Act of 1934 licensed broadcasters on the condition that they serve "the public interest, convenience, and necessity".

Periodical publication of written information about current events, typically issued daily or weekly. Newspapers cover politics, business, sport, art, science and religion, and often include opinion columns, weather forecasts, obituaries, [[Crossword|crossword]] and [[Sudoku|sudoku]] puzzles, editorial cartoons and comic strips. Most are businesses that pay their expenses with subscriptions, newsstand sales and [[Advertising|advertising]]. Newspapers developed in the 17th century as information sheets for merchants, and by the early 19th century many cities in Europe and the Americas published them. Traditionally printed on cheap newsprint, most are now also published on [[Website|websites]], and some have abandoned their print versions entirely. Papers with high editorial independence and large circulation are viewed as newspapers of record.

Semiaquatic [[Salamander|salamander]] in the subfamily Pleurodelinae. Unlike other members of the family Salamandridae, newts alternate between aquatic and terrestrial habitats. They [[Metamorphosis|metamorphose]] through three life stages: aquatic [[Larva|larvae]], a terrestrial juvenile called an eft, and an adult. Adults have lizard-like bodies and return to water each year to breed. Newts are found in North America, Europe, North Africa and Asia. They are threatened by [[Habitat|habitat]] loss, fragmentation and [[Pollution|pollution]], and at least one species, the Yunnan lake newt, has been considered extinct since 1979.

American Republican politician and speaker of the [[United States House of Representatives]] (1995–99). Representing [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]]'s 6th district from 1979, he co-wrote the "Contract with America" and led the Republican victory in the 1994 congressional elections. [[Time (magazine)|Time]] named him "Man of the Year" in 1995. As speaker he oversaw welfare reform in 1996, and the House impeached President [[Bill Clinton]] on a party-line vote. He withdrew from the 2012 Republican presidential race and endorsed [[Mitt Romney]]. Since 2020 he has supported [[Donald Trump]]'s claims of election fraud.

Law of physics stating that any two particles attract each other with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. [[Isaac Newton]] published it in *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica* on July 5, 1687. In the equation F = Gm₁m₂/r², F is the force, m₁ and m₂ are the masses, r is the distance between their centers, and G is the gravitational constant, 6.674×10⁻¹¹ m³⋅kg⁻¹⋅s⁻². The law resembles [[Coulomb's law]] for electric forces, and both are inverse-square laws. [[Henry Cavendish]] first tested it in a laboratory in 1798. The law was superseded by [[General relativity|general relativity]], but it remains an excellent approximation in most applications. Relativity is needed for extreme accuracy, very strong gravitational fields or small distances, such as [[Mercury (planet)|Mercury]]'s orbit around the [[Sun]].

Root-finding algorithm for real-valued functions, also called the Newton–Raphson method after [[Isaac Newton]] and Joseph Raphson. Starting from an initial guess near a root, it uses the tangent line of the function's graph to find a better approximation: xₙ₊₁ = xₙ − f(xₙ)/f′(xₙ). The method requires the [[Derivative|derivative]] of the function, and the number of correct digits roughly doubles with each step. An equivalent method appears in [[Hero of Alexandria]]'s *Metrica* (1st–2nd century CE), and it is often called Heron's method.

Unit of force in the [[International System of Units]] (SI), symbol N. One newton is the force that accelerates a mass of one [[Kilogram|kilogram]] by one [[Metre|meter]] per second squared, or 1 kg⋅m/s². The unit is named after [[Isaac Newton]] in recognition of his second law of motion, F = ma. In 1948 the 9th General Conference on Weights and Measures adopted the name newton. At average gravity on Earth, a kilogram mass exerts about 9.81 N. Large forces are expressed in kilonewtons, where 1 kN = 1000 N.

Brazilian footballer, a forward and attacking midfielder for Santos, which he also captains. He led Santos to the [[Copa Libertadores]] title in 2011. He joined [[FC Barcelona]] in 2013, forming the MSN attacking trio with [[Lionel Messi]] and [[Luis Suárez (Uruguayan footballer)|Luis Suárez]]. In 2017 he moved to Paris Saint-Germain in a world-record €222 million transfer, and he won several [[Ligue 1]] titles. He is Brazil's all-time top goalscorer and won Olympic gold in 2016, the nation's first. He retired from international football in 2026.

Protection deity in [[Taoism]], [[Buddhism]], [[Confucianism]] and Chinese folk religion, sometimes called Nezha the Crown Prince. He developed as a localization of Nalakuvara, a Hindu yaksha, as Buddhist Jataka tales spread into China. In the novel [[Investiture of the Gods]] (Fengshen Yanyi), Nezha is born during the [[Shang dynasty]] as the son of the military commander Li Jing. After he kills the son of the Dragon King of the East Sea, a dispute that reaches the Jade Emperor, he is reconciled with his father. He is known as the Third Lotus Prince, and in folk religion he is revered as a protector of children.

Kenyan author and academic, described as East Africa's leading novelist. He first wrote in English, with novels including *The River Between* and *Weep Not, Child*, before switching mainly to Gikuyu and becoming a strong advocate for literature in African languages. He founded the Gikuyu-language journal *Mũtĩiri*. In 1977 his play *Ngaahika Ndeenda*, co-written with Ngũgĩ wa Mirii, was shut down by the Kenyan government six weeks after opening, and he was imprisoned. He later fled Kenya and taught at [[Yale University]] and [[New York University]] before becoming a distinguished professor at the University of California, Irvine. He was frequently regarded as a likely candidate for the Nobel Prize in Literature.

Protected area and [[World Heritage Site]] in northeastern [[Tanzania]], named after the Ngorongoro Crater, a large volcanic [[Caldera|caldera]]. The area is home to the Great Migration of millions of [[Wildebeest|wildebeest]], zebras and gazelles, and its western portion abuts [[Serengeti National Park]]. It also contains Olduvai Gorge, one of the world's most important paleoanthropological sites. [[Maasai people|Maasai]] pastoralists live in the area, and the 2009 Ngorongoro Wildlife Conservation Act restricted settlement and farming in the crater, displacing many of them. The Ngorongoro Conservation Area Authority, an arm of the Tanzanian government, manages the area. It became a [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Site in 1979, and it drew 752,232 tourists in 2023.

Last Vietnamese dynasty, which ruled independently from 1802 until the French protectorate began in 1883, and nominally until 1945. Its rule extended into modern Southern Vietnam, [[Cambodia]] and Laos. Gia Long took the throne in 1802 after ending the Tây Sơn dynasty. From 1858 France gradually absorbed the dynasty's territory: Cochinchina became a French colony in 1862, and in 1887 Cochinchina, Annam, Tonkin and Cambodia were grouped as [[French Indochina]]. The dynasty remained the formal emperors of Annam and Tonkin until [[World War II]]. In 1945 Japan overthrew the French administration, and the dynasty ended with the abdication of Emperor Bảo Đại after the [[Surrender of Japan|surrender of Japan]] and the August Revolution, ending its 143-year rule. Its emperors built the Citadel of [[Huế]].

Group of three waterfalls at the southern end of the Niagara Gorge, spanning the border between [[Ontario]] and [[New York (state)|New York]]. The largest, Horseshoe Falls, straddles the international border and stands about 57 m (187 ft) high. The American Falls and Bridal Veil Falls lie in the United States. Formed by the Niagara River, which drains [[Lake Erie]] into [[Lake Ontario]], the falls have the highest flow rate of any waterfall in North America. At peak daytime tourist hours, more than 168,000 m³ (5.9 million ft³) of water goes over the crest every minute. The falls are about 27 km (17 miles) northwest of [[Buffalo, New York|Buffalo]] and are a valuable source of hydroelectric power. They formed when glaciers receded at the end of the Wisconsin glaciation and water from the newly formed [[Great Lakes]] carved a path over the Niagara Escarpment.

Capital and largest city of [[Niger]], on the left bank of the [[Niger River]]. Settled by Fula, Zarma, Maouri and Songhai peoples, it was the site of a French military post established by Captain Henri Salaman in 1901, and it has been the capital since the colonial era. Zarma and Hausa, both widely spoken, serve as [[Lingua franca|lingua francas]]. Most residents follow Islam, with a Christian minority. Commerce dominates the economy, largely in the informal sector. Niamey is one of the hottest major cities in the world and is prone to drought and flooding. The Niger River is the city's only permanent river and its sole source of [[Water supply|municipal water]]. Abdou Moumouni University is Niger's most important university.
